title_original: Christie’s Hauls In $289.4M at London Sales, Led by $41.8M Kandinsky
excerpt_original: Blue-chip material sold briskly, while some other material struggled. Records were reset for Liubov Popova and Portia Zvavahera.

blocks.text: On Wednesday night in London, Christie’s 20th- and 21st-century evening auctions brought in £219 million, or $289.4 million, a solid though not spectacular result at the low end of the house’s estimates. The top lot was an early Wassily Kandinsky painting, which went for an above-estimate £31.6 million ($41.8 million).

The two-part affair kicked off with the expansive and dependably colorful collection of Peter Simon , the founder of British fashion retailers Monsoon and Accessorize , which made £107.5 million, or $142.3 million.

Next up was a multiple-owner sale with 45 lots by modern and contemporary giants, about a third of which were backed by third-party guarantees. It achieved $147 million, clearing its low estimate of $116 million. Five lots were withdrawn from that section, and seven works were bought in. Last year’s comparable sale at Christie’s earned a seven-year high of $143 million across 61 lots. (Totals include fees, unless noted, while estimates do not.)

“Here it is, the most important early Kandinsky to come to auction,” auctioneer Adrien Meyer said, introducing Das bunte Leben (1907), a busy pastoral scene that blends Russian folk art with avant-garde sensibilities. It arrived at Christie’s after a decades-long Nazi restitution battle. In 2023, the German state returned it to the heirs of the German-Jewish collector Hedwig Lewenstein-Weyermann .
After steady bidding, the lot was eventually won by a client of Maria Los , Christie’s head of client advisory for the Americas.

blocks.alt: a folk scene with losts of people and a hill in the background

blocks.text: Wassily Kandinsky, Das bunte Leben , 1907. Photo: courtesy Christie’s.

Piet Mondrian ’s Composition III (Komposition No. XIII) , 1920, was also hotly anticipated, coming from his Paris years, when the Dutchman was honing his trademark approach to Neoplasticism. It was the work’s first appearance at auction: For much of the past century it had been on loan to German museums, including the Brandenburg State Museum of Modern Art and the Museum of Applied Arts Cologne. It surpassed its low estimate, hammering at $28.4 million—$33.4 million with fees.

The work is one of only eight that Mondrian completed in 1920, and five of those hang in major museums. The previous record for a work of that vintage was the $8.9 million paid for another example at Christie’s Paris in 2009.

blocks.alt: a painting composed of red, yellow, white, and gray rectangles

blocks.text: Piet Mondrian, Composition III , 1920. Photo: courtesy Christie’s.
Several more modestly priced works prompted fervent bidding.

David Hockney ’s Dog Painting 17 (1995)—“This is Stanley , his favorite dog,” Meyer said—provoked a four-way contest that ran for several minutes. It eventually jumped its presale high estimate to sell for $4.67 million.

Likewise, a pair of Josef Albers works that opened the second portion of the night, R-I d-1 (1968) and Study for Homage to the Square: Warm Silence (1971), saw very competitive bidding. Both eased past their high estimates, going for $779,000 and $983,000, respectively.

“It was a relatively solid sale given the current market environment,” Betsy Bickar , head of Citi Wealth ’s art advisory, told me in an email. “The sale felt broadly reflective of the current market: rare, high-quality blue-chip or undervalued works sold solidly with active bidding, while results across the remainder were more uneven.”

That dynamic was also visible in the 41-lot Simon collection, which totaled $147.1 million against a high estimate of $152 million—the largest estimate ever given to a single-owner collection at Christie’s London.

The event came in the wake of other London sales from fellow mega-collectors, like Joe Lewis , whose Modigliani -led collection netted $392.6 million at Sotheby’s , and Anita and Poju Zabludowicz , who did a $20 million collection pruning at Christie’s.
No works were withdrawn from the Simon section, and only one, a Frank Auerbach portrait, was bought in.

A Mondrian was also a marquee lot here, Composition A, with Double Line and Yellow (1935), which was first acquired by James Johnson Sweeney , the serial museum director who championed the painter in the United States. It was last at auction at Christie’s London in 2014, when it was bought in on a high estimate of $13.5 million. Here, it finished at $12.9 million.

blocks.alt: a twisting figure with a black door in a painting

blocks.text: Francis Bacon, Figure in Movement , 1978. Photo: courtesy Christie’s.

The other heavy hitter was Francis Bacon ’s Figure in Movement (1978), a blur of contorted flesh hovering before a dark portal. It is part of a cathartic grouping of paintings Bacon made following the death of his lover George Dyer . The record for a work from that series is $52.2 million, which was paid for Figure in Movement (1976) at Christie’s New York in 2023 . This one sold for $22.7 million, just above its low estimate, earning some muffled applause from the audience.

blocks.alt: a blue and green forest scene from above

blocks.text: Hurvin Anderson, Last House , 2013. Photo: courtesy Christie’s.

There was a much warmer reception when Liubov Popova ’s Painterly Architectonic (1918) sold. “It’s very rare and very early, you won’t find another like it,” Meyer announced. Bidders agreed, soon pushing the work by the Constructivist pioneer well past her previous auction record. The radical architectonic vision ultimately went to Alex Rotter , global president at Christie’s, for $10.1 million, more than double its high estimate.
The opening lot of the Simon portion, Portia Zvavahera ‘s This is where I travelled (2020), also set an artist record, going for $407,000.

Another well-contested work was Hurvin Anderson ’s dense tropical Last House (2013), which displays the vibrant patterning for which Simon’s collection is known. It sold for $7.55 million, above a high estimate of $3.9 million. The British artist’s survey earlier this year at Tate Britain couldn’t have hurt demand.

Jeff Koons ’s Baroque Egg with Bow (Blue/Turquoise), dated 1994–2008, had a less spectacular showing. The piece, which once stood inside Monsoon’s London headquarters, hammered for below its low estimate and made only $1.94 million with fees. Simon bought the enormous crinkly-looking Easter egg for $4.1 million at Christie’s London in 2012.

Overall, though, the results were mostly good news for the trade. “The audience, composed largely of art-market participants, seemed ready to celebrate incremental signs of strength,” Bickar said. “Perhaps reflecting a growing sense that a broader market rebound is becoming more plausible.”
